=== CALL C0415 ===
Gareth: Alright? Can you hear me okay?
Martijn: Yes, fine. Martijn. I'm in Walthamstow.
Gareth: Gareth, Taunton. Nice to meet you. I'll say now, if you hear a beep in the background it's the machine behind me, not my laptop. I'm not on it at the moment, but it likes to remind me it exists.
Martijn: I saw it in the photo. Dialysis?
Gareth: Yeah, home haemodialysis. Five times a week, about four hours a go. I've got the spare room set up as a sort of mini unit. Been on it since my kidneys packed in, so, erm, three years. Sorry, closer to three and a half now.
Martijn: That's a lot of hours.
Gareth: It is. You get used to it. I listen to the cricket mostly. Somerset, if anyone's still asking.
Martijn: I don't follow cricket. I saw the ICE certificate as well. You're a civil engineer?
Gareth: Was. Well, still chartered, I keep the membership going. Drainage and flood defence, mainly, for a consultancy down here. Hydraulic modelling, planning stuff, site meetings in wellies. Had to stop when I went on dialysis. You've got the hard hat, so I'm guessing...?
Martijn: Structural. Associate director at a consultancy in Farringdon. Mostly residential, some mixed-use.
Gareth: Ah, proper buildings. What's on your desk at the moment?
Martijn: A basement extension under a Victorian terrace. The neighbours are difficult and the ground is worse. Groundwater higher than the survey said.
Gareth: Course it is. That's my world, that. Nobody believes the groundwater figures till they've dug the hole. Have you got a decent site investigation, or is it one borehole and a prayer?
Martijn: Two boreholes. Both in the garden, not near the party wall. So, er, sort of a prayer.
Gareth: [laughs] Classic. You'll be designing for the worst case then.
Martijn: I always design for the worst case. The architect thinks I'm being difficult.
Gareth: They always do. I used to have one who'd put a swale through the middle of everything because it looked nice on the render. Then wonder why the levels didn't work.
Martijn: Yes. Pretty drawings.
Gareth: How did you find the puzzle bit at the start?
Martijn: Fine. One of the sequence questions was badly worded. There were two valid answers.
Gareth: The one with the numbers going up by odd steps? I thought that. I put the one I thought they wanted rather than the one I thought was right.
Martijn: I put the right one.
Gareth: [laughs] Fair enough. So, are you from the Netherlands? I'm getting a bit of an accent.
Martijn: Dordrecht. I came for two years. That was twenty-three years ago.
Gareth: Dordrecht. That's all water management, isn't it, round there? Proper envy territory for a flood bloke. I did Amsterdam and Copenhagen before I got ill. Spent most of the time looking at the canals, Hannah'll tell you.
Martijn: Most Dutch people don't think about it. It's just there. My father was a ship's engineer, so I grew up with the river.
Gareth: Do you go back much?
Martijn: A few times a year. Train, I don't fly if I can avoid it. Do you still travel, with the machine?
Gareth: Bits. You have to book holiday dialysis at a unit in advance, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so, you know, fingers crossed. Then I'd like to get back in, maybe freelance, reviewing flood risk assessments.
Martijn: There's demand. Most of the ones I see are poor.
Gareth: That's what I'm counting on.

Joanne: Oh, that's not bad advice, that. My Becky was exactly the same at fourteen, wouldn't give me the time of day. Now she rings me from Leeds three times a week to moan about her boss.
Martijn: That's reassuring.
Joanne: They come back round. Just keep turning up, do you know what I mean? Even if they're mardy.
Martijn: Mardy?
Joanne: [laughs] Sulky. Grumpy. It's a Nottingham thing.
Martijn: I'll use it. She'll be mardy that I know the word.

Abena: Abena. Croydon.

Abena: Mm. You work in a school, she said?

Agnieszka: No. But is something. My mum says, you have your life, is okay. I don't believe her. [laughs]

Abena: Every two or three years. I'm building a house there, slowly, for when I retire. Block by block, when there's money.

=== CALL C0424 ===

Sana: Not yet. Everyone asks me that today. [laughs] My mother-in-law asks every day. It's fine.

Abena: Then you can't have mine. It's tomatoes, goat, pepper. That's it.
Gareth: [laughs] Probably for the best. Smells better than my freezer, I bet.

Agnieszka: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.

I was so stressed, honestly. I was thinking, is this a test, like, will they think I'm stupid? I did like half of it and then the timer was finished.

But it's part-time, so like three, four shifts. And they keep changing my shift, it got changed again this week. I'm so tired.

Abena: I'm good at it. Like is another thing. The families trust me because I tell them the truth. If their mother is going down, I tell them. Some managers don't like that. That's it.

Abena: Ghana. Kumasi.
Sana: Oh nice! Do you go back?
Abena: Every two, three years. I'm saving now. The flights are crazy.

I'm doing a course as well, lashes, beauty. I want to do my own business on Instagram, like bookings, a proper room.
Abena: You finished the course?
Sana: Erm... not yet. [laughs] Nearly. Sort of halfway.

calls.C0415:
Gareth: Alright? Can you hear me okay?
Martijn: Yes, fine. Martijn. I'm in Walthamstow.
Gareth: Gareth, Taunton. Nice to meet you. I'll say now, if you hear a beep in the background it's the machine behind me, not my laptop. I'm not on it at the moment, but it likes to remind me it exists.
Martijn: I saw it in the photo. Dialysis?
Gareth: Yeah, home haemodialysis. Five times a week, about four hours a go. I've got the spare room set up as a sort of mini unit. Been on it since my kidneys packed in, so, erm, three years. Sorry, closer to three and a half now.
Martijn: That's a lot of hours.
Gareth: It is. You get used to it. I listen to the cricket mostly. Somerset, if anyone's still asking.
Martijn: I don't follow cricket. I saw the ICE certificate as well. You're a civil engineer?
Gareth: Was. Well, still chartered, I keep the membership going. Drainage and flood defence, mainly, for a consultancy down here. Hydraulic modelling, planning stuff, site meetings in wellies. Had to stop when I went on dialysis. You've got the hard hat, so I'm guessing...?
Martijn: Structural. Associate director at a consultancy in Farringdon. Mostly residential, some mixed-use.
Gareth: Ah, proper buildings. What's on your desk at the moment?
Martijn: A basement extension under a Victorian terrace. The neighbours are difficult and the ground is worse. Groundwater higher than the survey said.
Gareth: Course it is. That's my world, that. Nobody believes the groundwater figures till they've dug the hole. Have you got a decent site investigation, or is it one borehole and a prayer?
Martijn: Two boreholes. Both in the garden, not near the party wall. So, er, sort of a prayer.
Gareth: [laughs] Classic. You'll be designing for the worst case then.
Martijn: I always design for the worst case. The architect thinks I'm being difficult.
Gareth: They always do. I used to have one who'd put a swale through the middle of everything because it looked nice on the render. Then wonder why the levels didn't work.
Martijn: Yes. Pretty drawings.
Gareth: How did you find the puzzle bit at the start?
Martijn: Fine. One of the sequence questions was badly worded. There were two valid answers.
Gareth: The one with the numbers going up by odd steps? I thought that. I put the one I thought they wanted rather than the one I thought was right.
Martijn: I put the right one.
Gareth: [laughs] Fair enough. So, are you from the Netherlands? I'm getting a bit of an accent.
Martijn: Dordrecht. I came for two years. That was twenty-three years ago.
Gareth: Dordrecht. That's all water management, isn't it, round there? Proper envy territory for a flood bloke. I did Amsterdam and Copenhagen before I got ill. Spent most of the time looking at the canals, Hannah'll tell you.
Martijn: Most Dutch people don't think about it. It's just there. My father was a ship's engineer, so I grew up with the river.
Gareth: Do you go back much?
Martijn: A few times a year. Train, I don't fly if I can avoid it. Do you still travel, with the machine?
Gareth: Bits. You have to book holiday dialysis at a unit in advance, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so, you know, fingers crossed. Then I'd like to get back in, maybe freelance, reviewing flood risk assessments.
Martijn: There's demand. Most of the ones I see are poor.
Gareth: That's what I'm counting on.
calls.C0416:
Sana: Hiya! Oh, you look exactly like your picture, the same smile!
Agnieszka: [laughs] Hiya. Well, is the same face, yeah. I'm Agnieszka. Wolverhampton.
Sana: Sana, I'm in Bolton. Sorry, can you say your name again? I want to say it right.

Agnieszka: Yeah, from Łódź. I'm here since 2006, so, long time now. I work in school office, primary school in Tettenhall. Attendance, dinner money, angry dads at front desk, you know?
Sana: Oh my God, angry dads. [laughs] Do you shout back?
Agnieszka: No, no. I just say, okay, give it me, what is the problem, and usually is something small. A coat. Somebody lost a coat and is like end of the world.

Agnieszka: What course?
Sana: Lashes, beauty. I want to do my own business, mehndi and lashes, from home, Instagram. But I started it last year and, erm, it's sort of still sitting there.
Agnieszka: Yeah, no, she's right. But also, you know, life. When I came here I had degree in economics and I was cleaning offices for two years. Six in the morning, hoovering. You don't always do the plan when you want.
Sana: Really? With a degree?
Agnieszka: Yeah. My English wasn't good enough then, and nobody cares what is your degree from Poland. Then I did bookkeeping course at college here, then school job. So is fine. Slowly, slowly.
Sana: That's so good though. My English also was bad when I came, I did ESOL at Bolton College. The first years I was, honestly, so lonely, I didn't go anywhere except my mother-in-law's.
Agnieszka: I understand that. Very much. Is your family here?
Sana: Only my husband's family. My mum and my sisters are in Lahore. I do voice notes with my sisters all day, all day. And video calls, and then after I cry. [laughs] Every time. My husband says why you call if you cry?
Agnieszka: [laughs] Men. My mum is in Łódź, on her own now, seventy-eight. We do WhatsApp video every few days. And I think, should I bring her here? But she don't speak English, her friends are there, her church. Is difficult.
Sana: Yeah... that's hard. My mum would hate the weather here anyway. Lahore is so hot, and here it's like, rain, rain, rain.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Same in Poland but colder. Winter in Łódź, minus fifteen. Here they close school for little bit of snow.
Sana: What do you do at the weekend then, if you're not at school?

Agnieszka: [laughs] Everybody did that once. Do you cook?
Sana: Every day, because Imran wants Pakistani food. Karahi, daal, roti. But I'm bored, I always say let's get Nando's. And at work I say tea now, not dinner, and barm. Barm cake. Do you say that?
Agnieszka: No, here is bap! I buy baps for my daughter for lunch. When I came I didn't know any of these words. Bap, cob, barm, is all the same bread.
Sana: [laughs] English is so confusing, yaar.

Martijn: Hello. Martijn. Walthamstow.
Abena: Abena. Thornton Heath.
Martijn: Did you do the puzzles at the start?
Abena: Yes. Some of them were badly made. The shapes.
Martijn: The sequences too. One had two correct answers.
Abena: I didn't count. I just put something and moved on. You complained?
Martijn: No. I'll put it in the survey.
Abena: Good. Somebody should tell them.

Martijn: How many a week?

Martijn: Yes. It's better they know.
Abena: Of course it's better. They are paying. They should know.
Martijn: How many hours do you do in total?
Abena: About forty, forty-eight. You?
Martijn: Fifty, fifty-five. Er, mostly my choice. I don't send drawings I'm not happy with.
Abena: Fifty-five and nobody makes you. That's your problem then.
Martijn: [pause] Yes. My ex-wife said that.
Abena: Mm. Mine left for a woman from our church. So. Everybody has something.
Martijn: Yes.
Abena: You have children?
Martijn: A daughter, fourteen. Every other weekend and one night in the week.

Abena: I already write to him. He doesn't answer.

Sana: Aww, she's so pretty. Same place every year? You don't want to try somewhere new? I want to go Maldives, or Turkey, for the photos, you know, the water villas.
Martijn: No. She likes it, I know where everything is, and we take the train. I don't like flying.
Sana: Oh, I love flying! Well, not the flying, the airport, the duty free. We went Dubai once, me and my husband and his sister. The malls, oh my God, so big you need a car inside. [laughs]
Martijn: I've heard. Too big for me.
Sana: Does your daughter like makeup and that? Because fourteen, all the girls are on TikTok doing the routines.
Martijn: Er, yes. More than before. I don't really know what she's watching. She doesn't tell me much now.
Sana: That's normal, honestly. My little sister was like that, she wouldn't talk to my mum for like a whole year. Now they're best friends. You should ask her to show you her makeup stuff, girls love that, explaining everything. My sister made me watch a forty-minute video about skincare once.
Martijn: Forty minutes.
Sana: Yeah! But it made her happy, you know.
Martijn: That's a sensible idea, actually. I'll try it.
Sana: Really? [laughs] Okay! Tell her a girl from Bolton said.
Martijn: Do you have children?
Sana: No, not yet. Erm... not yet. Everyone asks. My mother-in-law asks every day nearly. [laughs]
Martijn: Sorry. I didn't mean to pry.
Sana: No, no, it's fine! It's a normal question.
calls.C0419:
Agnieszka: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.
Gareth: Alright? Gareth, Taunton. Nice to meet you.
Agnieszka: You too. Can I ask, that machine behind you, is dialysis, yeah? I saw in the photo.
Gareth: Yeah, home haemodialysis. Five sessions a week, about four hours each. The spare room's basically a little clinic now. Kidneys gave up about three and a half years ago.
Agnieszka: Four hours, five times. That's like a part-time job.
Gareth: [laughs] That's what I tell people. Pays worse, mind. I was a civil engineer before, flood defence mostly, but I had to stop.
Agnieszka: And you do it yourself, the needles and everything?
Gareth: Yeah. You get trained up at the unit for a few months, then they let you loose. Hannah, my partner, she helps set up on bad days. She's a SENCo at a primary school, so she's well used to looking after people.
Agnieszka: Oh, primary! I work in primary school office, in Tettenhall. Front desk, attendance, dinner money. So I know the SENCo, always running, always with papers.
Gareth: That's her. Her marking and paperwork lives on our kitchen table. I have to eat round it.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Our SENCo is same. Is the busiest person in the school, I think. So what do you eat? Is a special diet, no?
Gareth: Very. Low potassium, low phosphate, and I can only drink about a litre a day. I weigh everything and log it on an app. Bit obsessive, but it works.
Agnieszka: Potassium, so no tomatoes? Oh no. I grow tomatoes, this year so many, I was going to say I send you some.
Gareth: [laughs] I'm allowed a few. A slice or two, carefully. Bananas are the real enemy. And I miss proper cheddar. And crisps. And a cold pint. Being thirsty all day is the worst bit, honestly.
Agnieszka: That's hard. My husband, he can't go two hours without tea.
Gareth: It does sort of focus the mind. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so that's the hope.
Agnieszka: Family can't give, like a brother or something?
Gareth: My brother got tested. Wasn't a match. So, erm, it's the list.
Agnieszka: Okay. I hope it comes soon. I mean it.
Gareth: Cheers. Appreciate that. What about you, you've been here a while? I'm guessing Poland?
Agnieszka: Yeah, Łódź. Since 2006. First two years I was cleaning offices, then college, bookkeeping, then the school. Now is eighteen years, my kids grew up here. My son is at uni in Leeds, my daughter doing A-levels.
Gareth: That's a proper journey. Do you get back much?
Agnieszka: Once, twice a year, my mum is there. I drive sometimes, sometimes fly from Birmingham. I don't mind long drives.
Gareth: Lucky. Travel's a whole spreadsheet for me now. I have to book dialysis at a unit wherever we go, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go.
Agnieszka: But you still go. That's the important thing.
Gareth: Yeah, that's how Hannah puts it. And we take the dog. Biscuit, old Border terrier. Refuses to walk if it's raining, so not much use in the Lakes.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Clever dog. He knows.
Gareth: He does. Sits down on the canal path and just looks at me.
calls.C0420:
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, there you are. I'm Joanne, I'm in Arnold, just outside Nottingham. How's your day going?
Abena: Abena. Thornton Heath. It's okay. I'm off today.
Joanne: Oh, lovely, a day off. I thought you looked like you'd just come off shift in your photo. Uniform and that.
Abena: That photo was after a twelve-hour day. I'm a senior care assistant, care home for older people.
Joanne: Twelve hours, bless you. I do part-time in a primary school office, mornings mostly, so I've got no right to moan, but I do anyway. [laughs] Photocopier jams every Monday, without fail.
Abena: Hm. Everybody's photocopier jams.
Joanne: [laughs] Universal truth, that. So what are you doing with your day off then?
Abena: Cooking. Light soup, goat, for the week. And I have a damp problem in my bathroom, my landlord won't fix it. One of the men on this study, the Dutch engineer, told me to hold toilet paper to the fan, see if it pulls. So I'm going to do that.
Joanne: Oh, that's a good tip! I'm going to try that, our fan's been rattling for months. Steve's an electrician and he still hasn't looked at it. Cobbler's children, isn't it.
Abena: Same everywhere.
Joanne: Can I ask you something, being in care? My mum's got early dementia. I go round three times a week. Some days she's fine, and some days she gets really agitated in the afternoon and accuses me of moving her things. I never know what to do.
Abena: Afternoons are common. We call it sundowning. Don't argue with her about the things. Even if you know you didn't move them. You say, okay, let's look together. Then you find it, or you make a tea, and she forgets.
Joanne: See, I always argue. I go, Mum, I didn't touch your purse, it's where you left it.
Abena: You are right, but being right doesn't help her. Also, lights on early, curtains closed before it gets dark. Shadows upset them. And a routine. Same time, same things.
Joanne: That's really helpful, honestly. Nobody's told me any of that. The GP just gives you leaflets.
Abena: Leaflets. [laughs] Yes. The families who do best are the ones who stop correcting.
Joanne: I'll try that. It does wear you down, you know, I'm practical about it but some days I drive home and just sit in the car for ten minutes.
Abena: That's normal. You have to look after yourself also. You have help? Brothers, sisters?
Joanne: My sister helps a bit. And Steve's good. The kids are grown up, Leeds and Derby, so they're not round the corner.
Abena: My son is in Leicester. Near you, no?
Joanne: Oh, not far at all, duck! Forty minutes down the M1. Does he come down to London much?
Abena: Christmas. He phones on Sundays. That's enough. He has his life.
Joanne: Yeah. I miss mine more than I let on, if I'm honest. House is too quiet.
Abena: Mm. Quiet is not so bad. You get used to it.
calls.C0421:
Sana: Hiya! Oh, hello! Can you hear me?
Gareth: Alright? Yeah, loud and clear. Gareth, I'm in Taunton.
Sana: Sana, Bolton. Erm, sorry, can I ask, that machine behind you, is it for the hospital, like?
Gareth: Sort of. It's a dialysis machine. My kidneys stopped working, so that does the job for them. Five times a week, four hours a go, in the spare room. Saves me trekking to the unit.
Sana: Oh my God. Four hours? What do you do all that time?
Gareth: Listen to the cricket, mostly. Somerset. County cricket, so it goes on for days, which is handy really.
Sana: Cricket! My husband is mad for cricket. Pakistan, obviously. When Pakistan play India, honestly, nobody is allowed to talk in the house. His dad is shouting at the telly, his mum is praying. [laughs]
Gareth: [laughs] That's the proper way to watch it. Does he play?
Sana: Sometimes, with his cousins in the park, tape ball. He says he's good. I don't know. [laughs] I don't understand it, the overs and everything.
Gareth: To be fair, half of England doesn't either. I could explain it, but we've only got three minutes and I'd need about forty.
Sana: [laughs] That's what the engineer man said about my sister's makeup video, forty minutes. Did you talk to him? Martijn?
Gareth: I did, first round. We were both engineers, so it was a lot of groundwater talk. Riveting stuff.
Sana: You're an engineer as well? Wow. Everybody in this study is so clever. I just pack parcels. [laughs]
Gareth: Was. Civil, flood defences. Had to stop when this lot started. So at the moment I'm, erm, mostly a professional patient. Nothing wrong with packing parcels, mind. Somebody's got to, or none of us get our stuff.
Sana: That's true! You know, at Christmas we're so busy, everybody's ordering dresses for parties. I'm knackered, my shift got changed again this week.
Gareth: They do that to you a lot?
Sana: All the time. But I swap with the girls, it's fine, I'm good at swapping. [laughs] Are you married? Sorry, is that rude?
Gareth: No, not rude. Partner, Hannah, eleven years. Not married. We always meant to, then the kidneys happened, and there's always another appointment.
Sana: Aww, no! You should do it. Even small, you know, nice. I do mehndi for weddings, henna on the hands. If you were in Bolton I would do Hannah's for free, honestly.
Gareth: [laughs] That's very kind. I'll pass it on. She'd probably like that, actually. She's always on at me to set a date.
Sana: Then set a date! When you get better.
Gareth: Well, I'm on the transplant list. Two years. If that comes through, then yeah, maybe. One project at a time, you know.
Sana: Inshallah it comes soon. I'll pray for you. I mean it.
Gareth: Cheers, Sana. That's kind of you.
Sana: Do you go out much, or no?
Gareth: Walk the dog along the canal. Biscuit. He's old and refuses to go out in the rain, so in Somerset that's about half the year.
Sana: [laughs] Bolton also! He would never go out in Bolton.
calls.C0422:
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, hang on, are you the Dutch engineer? With the toilet paper trick?
Martijn: Er, yes. Martijn. Walthamstow. Who told you that?
Joanne: Abena! I just had her. She's going home to test her fan tonight. I'm going to do ours an' all. I'm Joanne, by the way, Arnold, Nottingham.
Martijn: Good. Her landlord should fix it. It sounded like the building, not her.
Joanne: Well she won't let him off, I can tell you that. Lovely woman, mind. Gave me some proper good advice about me mum. So what do you build, then?
Martijn: Structures. Residential mostly. At the moment a basement under a Victorian terrace in Islington, which is going badly.
Joanne: Oh no. Why's that?
Martijn: Water in the ground. Neighbours. The architect. In that order, er, possibly reversed.
Joanne: [laughs] Sounds like parents' evening. I'm in a primary school office. I'm the one on the front desk dealing with the dads who've parked on the zigzags.
Martijn: Do you tell them to move?
Joanne: Every single morning, duck. Kindly. And then firmly.
Martijn: Good. Someone has to.
Joanne: What do you do when you're not digging basements?
Martijn: I cycle to work. Parkrun on Saturdays, Lloyd Park, when my daughter isn't staying.
Joanne: Oh, I do parkrun! Colwick Park, every Saturday. What's your time like?
Martijn: Twenty-four, twenty-five minutes. It's gone up a few seconds this year. I keep a spreadsheet.
Joanne: A spreadsheet! [laughs] I'm about thirty-five minutes, and that's me chatting all the way round. I only started after a cancer scare at fifty. It were fine in the end, but it gave me a kick up the backside, you know.
Martijn: That's a good reason. Better than mine. I just like the numbers.
Joanne: Well, whatever gets you out of bed. Then it's coffee after, that's the best bit for me, if I'm honest.
Martijn: I usually go home. Er, maybe I should stay for the coffee.
Joanne: You should! You'd get to know people. That's what it's for really. So you've got a daughter?
Martijn: Fourteen. She's quieter with me now. The girl from Bolton said I should ask her to show me her makeup videos.
Joanne: Oh, that's not bad advice, that. My Becky was exactly the same at fourteen, wouldn't give me the time of day. Now she rings me from Leeds three times a week to moan about her boss.
Martijn: That's reassuring.
Joanne: They come back round. Just keep turning up, do you know what I mean? Even if they're mardy.
Martijn: Mardy?
Joanne: [laughs] Sulky. Grumpy. It's a Nottingham thing.
Martijn: I'll use it. She'll be mardy that I know the word.
calls.C0423:
Agnieszka: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.
Abena: Abena. Croydon.
Agnieszka: Nice to meet you. I think you met Sana, from Bolton? She told me a lady told her off for not finishing her course. [laughs] Was you?
Abena: It was me. Somebody has to tell her. She's young. She keeps saying later, later.
Agnieszka: No, I agree with you. She's lovely girl, but she needs somebody to push a bit.
Abena: Mm. You work in a school, she said?
Agnieszka: Yeah, office, primary school. Twenty-five hours, term-time. Before that I was cleaning offices, two years, with degree in economics. So I told her also, plans don't always go when you want.
Abena: Cleaning with a degree. Yes. I know many like that. Nurses from Ghana doing cleaning. Here they don't care what you did at home.
Agnieszka: Exactly. You came when?
Abena: 2003. For my husband. I gave up a lot to come. He gave up nothing to leave. That's it.
Agnieszka: Oh. I'm sorry.
Abena: It's fine. Long time ago. You have a cross in your photo. You go to church?
Agnieszka: Yeah, Polish Mass, most Sundays. Honestly more for the people than the rules, you know? After Mass everybody is talking, coffee, cake. Is like small Poland for one hour.
Abena: I go to a Ghanaian Methodist church. Same, it's for the people. But every week they want money. New roof, new van, a building fund. The big men on the committee drive nice cars. I ask, where is the roof?
Agnieszka: [laughs] Every church is same, I think. Our priest also always has new project.
Abena: At least you can laugh. I sing in the choir, so I have to stay. Your family is in Poland?
Agnieszka: My mum, seventy-eight, on her own in Łódź. And my sister. I think a lot, should I bring her here. But she don't speak English. She would be lonely in my house all day.
Abena: My mother is in Kumasi. My sister looks after her. And I am here washing other people's mothers. Sometimes I think about that too much.
Agnieszka: Yeah. I understand. Is same feeling, you know? You look after everybody except your own.
Abena: Yes. Exactly that. I send money every month. It's not the same as being there.
Agnieszka: No. But is something. My mum says, you have your life, is okay. I don't believe her. [laughs]
Abena: Mine says the same. They are lying to make us feel better.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Probably. You go back?
Abena: Every two or three years. I'm building a house there, slowly, for when I retire. Block by block, when there's money.
Agnieszka: That's a good plan. Better than mine. I don't have a plan, I just say we'll see.
Abena: We'll see is also a plan. Sometimes.
calls.C0424:
Sana: Hiya! Oh, you've got the same smile as your picture!
Joanne: Hiya, duck! I'm Joanne, Arnold, near Nottingham. And look at you, your makeup's gorgeous. How do you get your eyeliner that even? Mine looks like a toddler's done it.
Sana: [laughs] Thank you! It's practice, honestly. And tape. You put tape here, at the corner, then draw. I'm Sana, I'm in Bolton.
Joanne: Tape! Who knew. My daughter Becky's the same as you, all the lashes and that. She'd love you. How are you finding all these calls?
Sana: Good! But I'm so nervous at the start of each one, like, what do I say? Then I just talk and talk. [laughs] You talked to the Dutch man? Martijn?
Joanne: I did! He told me about the girl from Bolton who said he should watch his daughter's makeup videos. Was that you?
Sana: That was me! Oh my God, he told you? [laughs] He was so serious, I thought he didn't like me.
Joanne: No, he took it to heart, I think. He's going to try it. And he learned the word mardy off me, so he's sorted.
Sana: Mardy? What is mardy?
Joanne: Sulky. Grumpy. Like a teenager when you tell them to put their phone down.
Sana: Ah, acha, we say that about my sister-in-law. [laughs] No, I'm joking. Bit. What do you do, Joanne?
Joanne: School office, primary. Front desk, dinner money, plasters, crying Year Twos. I love it really. What about you?
Sana: Packing, warehouse, online fashion. It's okay, it's money, you know. But what I really want, I want to do mehndi and lashes from home. I do mehndi for all the weddings in the family. My cousin's wedding is coming, I'm doing like twenty hands.
Joanne: Twenty! Your hands must be knackered.
Sana: Yes! And I don't even know what I'm wearing yet. I've got two outfits, one is a sort of emerald green, really heavy work on it, and one is peach. My mother-in-law likes the peach. I like the green.
Joanne: Wear the green, love. It's your wedding outfit, not hers. Well, it's your cousin's wedding, but you know what I mean.
Sana: [laughs] That's what I think! Okay, the green. You decided it.
Joanne: Glad to help. I'm useless at fashion, mind. Stripy top every day, Steve says I look like a deckchair.
Sana: No! It's nice, it's classic. Do you have a big family?
Joanne: Two grown-up kids, Becky in Leeds and Liam in Derby. And a deaf old dog called Pickle who only hears the treat tin. You got kids?
Sana: Not yet. Everyone asks me that today. [laughs] My mother-in-law asks every day. It's fine.
Joanne: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to be nosy. My mother-in-law used to do that and all, and I wanted to throw a cob at her.
Sana: A cob? What's a cob?
Joanne: A bread roll! What do you call them in Bolton?
Sana: Barm! I learned it at work. And the Polish lady, Agnieszka, she says bap. And you say cob. England, honestly, yaar, it's one bread and four names.
Joanne: [laughs] Don't get me started on what Becky's lot in Leeds call it. You're doing brilliant, you know. With the English and everything. I couldn't do what you've done, moving that far.
Sana: Aww, thank you, Joanne. That's really nice. Sometimes I think people look at me and think I'm, you know, not clever.
Joanne: Well, they're wrong, duck. You've chatted to everyone in this study and made them all like you. That's a skill.
calls.C0425:
Gareth: Alright? Gareth, Taunton.
Abena: Abena. Thornton Heath.
Gareth: Nice to meet you. Sorry, you'll see a machine behind me. Home dialysis. I'm not hooked up, so no alarms, hopefully.
Abena: I saw. How long?
Gareth: About three and a half years on dialysis. Five sessions a week, four hours each. Diagnosed at thirty-one, so, erm, it's been coming a while.
Abena: You do the needles yourself?
Gareth: Yeah. Took a few months of training at the unit. My partner helps on bad days.
Abena: That's good. We have residents on dialysis at the hospital, three days a week, the transport takes them. They come back grey. Doing it at home is better. More control.
Gareth: That's exactly why I wanted it. I like control. Bit of an engineer thing. Spreadsheet of my blood results, the lot.
Abena: [laughs] The Dutch man also has spreadsheets. You are the same.
Gareth: We did get on, to be fair. Two engineers moaning about groundwater.
Abena: Mm. Your partner. She is your carer now?
Gareth: Sort of, partly. She's a SENCo at a primary, works full-time, then comes home and helps me. I don't love that, if I'm honest. She didn't sign up for it.
Abena: Nobody signs up. But she stays. That means something.
Gareth: Yeah. She does. We never got married, mind. Sana from Bolton told me to set a date.
Abena: [laughs] Sana tells everybody what to do. And I tell her to finish her course. So we are even.
Gareth: [laughs] She offered to do Hannah's henna for free.
Abena: She would. She is kind. Talks too much, but kind. You are waiting for a kidney?
Gareth: Two years on the list. My brother was tested, wasn't a match.
Abena: He wanted to?
Gareth: [pause] Erm. He said he did. I'm not sure he was sorry when it came back no.
Abena: Hm. You can't make somebody give a kidney. But you can be upset. Both are true.
Gareth: Yeah. Hadn't thought of it like that. Cheers.
Abena: You worked before?
Gareth: Chartered civil engineer. Flood defences. Now I'm on benefits, which, you know, takes some getting used to. Went from the person everyone rang to the person filling in forms.
Abena: The forms are a job also. People think benefits is easy. You fill everything, they lose it, you fill again.
Gareth: [laughs] I've got quite good at it, truth be told. Know which number to ring and what to say.
Abena: Good. Use it. It's your right. You paid in.
Gareth: That's what Hannah says. What about you, long shifts?
Abena: Twelve hours, four or five days. Off today. Cooking light soup.
Gareth: I'd kill for a proper bowl of soup. Too much potassium in most of it.
Abena: Then you can't have mine. It's tomatoes, goat, pepper. That's it.
Gareth: [laughs] Probably for the best. Smells better than my freezer, I bet.
calls.C0426:
Agnieszka: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.
Martijn: Hello. Martijn. Walthamstow.
Agnieszka: Ah, you're the engineer with the toilet paper! Abena told me. She was very happy with this.
Martijn: Everyone seems to know. It's a simple test.
Agnieszka: Simple is the best. My husband would call a man, pay sixty pound, and the man does the toilet paper. [laughs]
Martijn: Probably. What do you do?
Agnieszka: School office, primary school. Front desk, attendance, dinner money. And now dinner money is on new app, so all the parents ring me to ask how is the app working. I don't know also.
Martijn: Who chose the app?
Agnieszka: The trust. Nobody asked us.
Martijn: That's usually how it works. You're from Poland?
Agnieszka: Łódź. Eighteen years here. You are Dutch, yeah? Sana said.
Martijn: Dordrecht. Twenty-three years. I came for two.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Everybody says this! Two years. My husband said also, two years, we save money, we go back. Now my kids are English.
Martijn: Do you think about going back?
Agnieszka: Sometimes. My mum is in Łódź, seventy-eight, alone. I think, I go back or I bring her here. But my daughter is doing A-levels, my son is in Leeds. Is not simple.
Martijn: No. Er, my father died when I was thirty-eight. I didn't get back in time. It was very fast.
Agnieszka: Oh. I'm sorry. That is my big fear, honestly.
Martijn: I'm not saying it to frighten you. Just, if you're thinking about it, think about it now. Not later.
Agnieszka: Yeah. No, you're right. Thank you for saying. Is not easy to say that to a stranger.
Martijn: It's easier with a stranger. [pause] Do you go back often?
Agnieszka: Once, twice a year. I drive sometimes, two days. I don't mind. Podcasts, coffee, is fine.
Martijn: I take the train. Eurostar, then to Rotterdam. Better than airports.
Agnieszka: Good. You miss Dutch food?
Martijn: The bread. British bread is too soft. Like a sponge.
Agnieszka: Yes! Thank you! There's a Polish shop on Dudley Road, proper bread, heavy, with seeds. If you lived in Wolverhampton I would tell you go there.
Martijn: Walthamstow has some Polish shops. I hadn't thought of it. I'll look.
Agnieszka: Rye bread. Is the best. Your daughter likes Dutch things?
Martijn: Hagelslag. Chocolate sprinkles on bread. She's fourteen, she complains about everything else.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Mine is seventeen. She complains also, but now sometimes she cooks with me. Is coming back slowly.
Martijn: Everyone keeps telling me that. Joanne said they come round if you keep turning up.
Agnieszka: She is right. You keep turning up. That's all.

C0418.line_text: Oh, erm, I think it's like ninety? Something like that. I don't really look, to be honest. The supervisor looks. I'm chatting with the girls, that's the best bit.
C0418.what: A man in a dark jacket walks past the open doorway to the hallway on the left behind her, taking the coat off the hook. Sana glances briefly over her shoulder towards him, then turns back to the camera still talking.
